title: Shortest Bridge
statement:
You are given a binary grid `grid` with `grid.length` rows and `grid[0].length` columns, where `grid[i][j] = 1` marks land and `0` marks water. Two land cells are connected when they share an edge (up, down, left or right), so the land forms islands. The grid is guaranteed to contain exactly two islands.

You may convert water into land, at a cost of one conversion per cell. Your goal is to make the two islands one connected piece: after the conversions, every land cell of the first island must reach every land cell of the second island by moving between edge-adjacent land cells. Cells that are already land stay land.

Return the minimum number of conversions needed, i.e. the smallest number of `0` cells that must become `1` so the two islands join. The converted cells must form a 4-connected water chain from a cell of one island to a cell of the other; converting cells that merely sit next to land without bridging does not help.

If the input breaks the two-island guarantee, then define the answer against island `A`, the island containing the topmost land cell (breaking ties by leftmost column): return the minimum number of conversions needed to connect `A` to any other land cell, or `-1` when the grid holds no land outside `A`.

Constraints: `2 <= grid.length <= 25`, `1 <= grid[i].length <= 25` and `0 <= grid[i][j] <= 1`.

constraints: Inputs are JSON-serializable values satisfying the bounds stated above.
hints: First decide which cells belong to the same island, because the shortest bridge is the water distance between the two sets.
One BFS per land cell of the first island already solves it; ask yourself which work those BFS runs are repeating.
Put every cell of the first island into the queue at distance 0 and expand once: the first land cell you reach from the other island gives the answer, adjusted by one.

editorial.approach: Both versions start by labelling island A with a flood fill from the first land cell in row-major order, using an explicit stack over the four edge neighbours. The brute force then runs an independent BFS from each cell of A, stopping the moment it lands on land outside A, and takes the smallest (distance - 1) found. The optimal version seeds one queue with every cell of A at distance 0 and expands layer by layer through the grid; the first land cell outside A that leaves the queue gives distance d, and d - 1 is the number of water cells crossed, so it can return immediately.
editorial.why_optimal: Multi-source BFS is BFS on the graph where all of A is contracted into a single super-source, so it visits each of the rows*cols cells once, giving O(rows*cols) total. The per-cell brute force repeats that entire traversal for every land cell of A, which is O(rows*cols) work per start in the worst case and O((rows*cols)^2) overall; on a 25x25 grid that is roughly 390k steps against a few hundred for the multi-source pass. Because every grid edge has unit cost, a BFS layer count is exactly the minimum number of cells to cross, so nothing cheaper than O(rows*cols) exists: the whole grid must be read.
editorial.pitfalls: Off-by-one on the bridge length: the BFS distance to the landing land cell counts that cell, so the water crossed is distance - 1, and the adjacent-islands case (distance 1) must return 0. Starting the flood fill from an arbitrary land cell instead of the first one is fine only if the same island is chosen in both implementations; picking the topmost-then-leftmost land cell keeps the two consistent. Expanding into land cells is required (island A cells are already at distance 0, and reaching island B ends the search), so blocking land during expansion breaks the connectivity. A grid with no land at all must return -1 rather than crashing on the seed search.
